claims.text: A conventionally synthesized W–Cu composite produced by powder metallurgy or casting has a homogeneous distribution of W and Cu phases.
Liquid-metal dealloying in molten Cu selectively dissolves Ti-rich interdendritic channels from a pre-alloyed precursor.
Selective dissolution of the Ti-rich channels produces an aligned refractory high-entropy-alloy phase embedded in the Cu matrix.
Aligned RHEA features enhance Cu connectivity in the composite.
Aligned RHEA features create more direct thermal-conduction pathways.
Aligned RHEA features structurally reinforce the composite.
A continuous, aligned RHEA–Cu phase enhances thermal transport.
The RHEA phase contributes mechanical robustness under extreme operating conditions.
The RHEA phase contributes irradiation resistance under extreme operating conditions.
Liquid-metal-dealloyed W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable conventionally processed W–Cu composite.
The thermal-conductivity improvement may be approximately 10–20%.
The liquid-metal-dealloyed composite will match the baseline composite's mechanical durability.
The liquid-metal-dealloyed composite will match the baseline composite's irradiation resistance.
The predicted performance will hold within temperature and irradiation regimes typical of advanced heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
Conditions outside the stated application regimes may alter dealloying effectiveness or the stability of the resulting microstructure.
